planting.note: Plant small nursery-grown transplants in spring into very well-drained, gravelly or sandy, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; growth is extremely slow, often only 1-3 inches a year, and container specimens establish far more reliably than direct seeding.

directions: Plant in lean, gravelly or sandy, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun and resist the urge to amend the planting hole or irrigate on a regular schedule; Joshua trees are adapted to the high-elevation Mojave Desert of California, Nevada, Arizona, and Utah, where winter cold and summer drought are both part of the plant's natural rhythm. This unmistakable, multi-branched arborescent yucca is topped with rosettes of stiff, dagger-like blue-green leaves and can eventually reach 15-40 feet with a gnarled, candelabra-like silhouette that takes many decades to develop. Established trees are extremely drought tolerant and cold hardy into the single digits Fahrenheit, but they are notoriously slow-growing and intolerant of poor drainage, soggy soil, or excess summer humidity, which makes them best suited to arid inland gardens rather than the humid Gulf Coast. Like other yuccas, the creamy, waxy spring flower clusters depend on the yucca moth (Tegeticula synthetica) for pollination, and mature trees are a keystone habitat feature in their native range.
sources: National Park Service (Joshua Tree National Park)
USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

common_name: Chaparral Yucca (Our Lord's Candle, Spanish Bayonet)

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring into sharply drained, rocky or sandy, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; site well away from paths, as the rigid, needle-tipped leaves are sharp enough to puncture skin.

directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, rocky to sandy soil in full sun and withhold supplemental irrigation once established; this chaparral and coastal-sage native from California and Baja California forms a dense, silvery-blue-green rosette of narrow, rigid, needle-tipped leaves that stays low and tidy for years before sending up its signature bloom spike. The plant is monocarpic, meaning each individual rosette flowers only once, in its case producing a dramatic 6-12 foot pole-like spike crowded with hundreds of creamy-white, purple-tinged, fragrant bell flowers over a period of weeks in late spring, after which that rosette dies; some populations (formerly classed as subsp. percursa) offset from the base and persist as clumps, while the typical form is usually solitary. Because of the years-long buildup to a single spectacular bloom, it is prized in xeriscape and rock-garden design as a long-term architectural accent rather than a repeat-flowering perennial. It tolerates poor, rocky soils and extended drought better than almost any other landscape yucca relative but resents heavy clay and wet winter feet.

planting.note: Plant well-callused stem segments (joints) in spring into very well-drained, sandy or gravelly, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; handle only with long tongs or a folded towel, as the barbed, easily detaching spines readily embed in skin and clothing.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, sandy or gravelly, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun, well away from foot traffic and pets; teddy bear cholla is a Sonoran and Mojave Desert native (Arizona, southeastern California, northwestern Mexico) forming a densely spined, silvery, teddy-bear-soft-looking trunk and branches that are anything but soft to the touch. Individual stem segments detach at the slightest touch and cling by barbed spines to passing animals or clothing, a dispersal strategy that gives the plant its 'jumping cholla' nickname, so it is best sited as a specimen or barrier planting away from paths. Established plants are extremely drought tolerant, thriving on rainfall alone in low-desert gardens, and bear small, pale greenish-yellow flowers in spring followed by spineless, tuberculate fruits. It is markedly more cold-sensitive than prickly pear and performs best in the warmest zones of the Southwest and coastal Gulf xeriscape, generally suffering damage below about 15-20 degrees Fahrenheit.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

common_name: Lace Hedgehog Cactus (Lace Cactus, Comb Hedgehog Cactus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, mineral cactus mix, or plant rooted offsets/transplants in spring into sharply drained, rocky or gravelly, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage matters more than soil fertility.

directions: Plant in sharply drained, rocky or gravelly, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; this low-growing, clump-forming cactus native to the limestone hills and prairies of Texas, Oklahoma, and northern Mexico is covered in densely interlacing, comb-like (pectinate) white to pinkish spines that lie flat against the stem in an intricate lattice pattern, giving rise to the common name. In mid-to-late spring, mature clumps produce a flush of large, satiny, magenta-pink flowers with a pale throat that can nearly obscure the plant, followed by small, spiny, edible red fruit. Among the most cold-hardy of the hedgehog cacti, it tolerates winter lows well below zero Fahrenheit provided the soil stays dry, and rot from wet, poorly drained soil is the single greatest threat to the species in cultivation. It is an excellent choice for rock gardens, gravel beds, and crevice plantings across the southern Great Plains and Texas Hill Country.

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets (pups) or transplants in spring into very well-drained, gritty, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; established clumps spread by offsets and can be divided at almost any time during the growing season.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty or rocky soil in full sun; this terrestrial bromeliad from the rocky highlands of southern Brazil forms a tight, symmetrical rosette of stiff, arching, olive-green to bronze leaves edged with sharp, recurved, saw-like teeth, gradually multiplying by offsets into a dense, spiny clump. In summer, wiry flower spikes rise well above the foliage bearing small, bright orange-yellow blooms that are a magnet for pollinators. It is one of the most cold-hardy dyckias in cultivation, tolerating brief dips into the low 20s and even upper teens Fahrenheit once established in sharply drained soil, which has made it a favorite architectural accent for Texas and Gulf Coast xeriscape and gravel gardens where true desert agaves may struggle with humidity. Unlike most bromeliads, dyckias are true sun- and drought-lovers with no central water-holding cup, and rot in poorly drained or overly rich soil is the main cultivation hazard.

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets or nursery divisions in spring into very well-drained, sandy or gritty soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; this hybrid does not come true from seed and is propagated only by division of its basal offsets.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, sandy or gritty soil in full sun, giving light afternoon shade in the hottest inland climates to preserve leaf color; 'Bloodspot' is one of the earliest and best-known intergeneric hybrids between Manfreda maculosa and Agave macroacantha, combining the soft, pliable, spineless (or nearly spineless) leaves of manfreda with the vigor and rosette form of agave. Its broad, gray-green leaves are heavily speckled with maroon-red spots that intensify with bright light and cooler temperatures, and unlike true century-plant agaves it is polycarpic, meaning the rosette does not die after flowering. Mangaves are notably faster-growing and more cold-tolerant than many pure agave species, and 'Bloodspot' in particular has become a staple of Texas and Gulf Coast xeriscape design for its dramatic color and reliable garden performance in well-drained beds and containers alike. Good air circulation and sharp drainage are essential, since rot rather than cold is the most common cause of failure.

common_name: Giant Carrion Flower (Zulu Giant, Starfish Flower)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant divisions after the danger of frost has passed, in gritty, very well-drained soil in bright light with some afternoon shade; allow cuttings to callus for several days before setting in the rooting medium.

directions: Plant in gritty, very well-drained soil in bright light with light afternoon shade in the hottest climates; this South African succulent forms a low, spreading mat of soft, four-angled, toothed, cactus-like stems that root easily wherever they touch the ground. In late summer it produces some of the largest flowers of any succulent grown in gardens, up to 10-14 inches across, star-shaped, and covered in fine wrinkled maroon-and-cream banding that mimics rotting flesh both in appearance and in scent, a strategy that lures flies as pollinators rather than bees. It is more cold-sensitive than most desert succulents and needs winter protection or container culture outside of zone 9-11, and unlike true cacti it appreciates slightly more regular moisture during active summer growth followed by a dry winter rest. Its sprawling habit makes it a striking, talking-point groundcover for raised beds, rock gardens, and container plantings in warm-climate xeriscapes.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, mineral cactus mix, or set out nursery transplants in spring into very well-drained, gravelly or sandy, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; growth from seed to a landscape-sized barrel is slow, typically many years.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gravelly or sandy, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; native to the arid hills of Hidalgo state in central Mexico, this compact barrel cactus is prized for its smooth, powdery blue-gray to gray-green stem and neat rows of golden-yellow spines that contrast sharply against the body color. Unlike many solitary barrel cacti, mature specimens readily offset from the base to form multi-headed clumps over time, adding to its sculptural appeal in xeriscape and container design. A ring of bright yellow, cup-shaped flowers appears at the crown in mid-to-late summer, followed by small yellow fruit. It tolerates brief cold snaps into the low-to-mid 20s Fahrenheit but is more cold-sensitive than the classic golden barrel (Echinocactus grusonii), so in zones 8b-9 it should be sited in a warm, sheltered, south-facing microclimate with protection from prolonged winter wet.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
